documents.abstract: As the Internet of Things (IoT) continues to grow exponentially, securing interconnected devices against evolving cyber threats has become paramount. This paper explores the development of an autonomous cyber defence system leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance intrusion detection for IoT networks. Traditional security measures fall short in resource-constrained, heterogeneous environments like IoT. Hence, we propose an AI-driven Intrusion Detection System (IDS) capable of real-time threat detection and autonomous response. Using a hybrid machine learning approach and reinforcement learning for automated mitigation, the system is evaluated on publicly available IoT security datasets. Results demonstrate improved detection accuracy, reduced false alarms, and efficient resource utilization. This research contributes to the advancement of intelligent, self-governing security mechanisms in IoT ecosystems.

Abstract Introduction Healthcare organisations worldwide are expected to investigate or review incidents that unintentionally harm or could cause harm. Investigation findings are presented in a written report, which is arguably a proxy measure for the quality of investigations. The report is an important document to be read and acted upon. The aims of this study were: 1) to design a tool to support the writing and review of healthcare safety investigation reports, and 2) to validate the content of the tool. Methods The study was conducted in two phases. Phase 1: The initial content of the tool was developed using relevant published literature and building consensus with 23 specialist participants from the United Kingdom and Australia. Phase 2: Content validity of the tool was assessed for relevance and clarity in two e-Delphi survey rounds with users of the tool. Using a 4-point scale, a median of 3 or 4 and an interquartile range of less than or equal to 1.5 were used to determine consensus. Results Phase 1: A tool containing 8 areas of review with accompanying descriptors was developed. For each area of review, a 3-point ordinal rating scale along with a comments box for formative self-assessment were included. Phase 2: At the end of the round 1 survey, there was consensus on all but one area of review in the tool. By the end of round 2 survey, consensus was reached on all areas of review. No additional areas of review were added and none were removed. Some descriptors were amended to improve clarity. Conclusion We co-designed and validated the content of a tool that can be used to inform the quality of safety investigation reports and learning in terms of a systems-based approach. The tool has multiple uses ranging from self-assessment for report writers to facilitating oversight of the quality of healthcare safety investigation reports. Future work could focus on building further evidence of the tool’s overall utility. What is already known on this topic – summarise the state of scientific knowledge on this subject before you did your study and why this study needed to be done The standard of healthcare safety investigation and reports internationally is known to be variable and often lacks the use of a Human Factors informed “systems approach”. A formal mechanism appears to be lacking to facilitate a review of, and provide feedback on, the standard of healthcare investigation reports, which arguably serves as a proxy for the overall quality of the investigation process. What this study adds – summarise what we now know as a result of this study that we did not know before To our knowledge, this is a first validated tool that has been developed to support self-assessment and oversight of written safety investigations reports and learning reviews. Key principles of a systems-based approach to healthcare safety investigations and learning reviews are incorporated into a single tool to guide self-assessment and improvement, where needed. How this study might affect research, practice or policy – summarise the implications of this study The tool supports organisational quality assurance or oversight mechanisms for monitoring, evaluating and improving the standard of investigation reports. As written report can act as a proxy measure for the quality of investigations, improving the standard of reports may inform the learning and associated action from healthcare safety investigations. Further research and evaluation are necessary to provide greater evidence of the utility of the tool.

Introduction Efficient packaging waste sorting is an important requirement for implementing circular economy strategies, yet many automated sorting solutions are designed for large-scale, high-throughput recycling facilities and are not well suited to small-batch industrial environments characterized by limited waste volumes, frequent material changes, and the need for rapid system reconfiguration. Methods This paper presents the design, implementation, and laboratory validation of a modular collaborative robotic workstation for small-batch packaging waste sorting. The proposed system integrates a collaborative robot, RGB-D vision system, conveyor-based material flow, and a ROS2-based control architecture within a unified perception–decision–manipulation framework. The perception pipeline combines class-agnostic segmentation using the Segment Anything Model (SAM) with lightweight MobileNetV2-based classification for material recognition and is extended with optional modules for geometric reasoning and damage assessment. The proposed architecture reduces dependence on task-specific segmentation training and provides semantic information relevant to grasp planning, safety-aware task allocation, and human–robot collaboration. Results The workstation was validated under controlled laboratory conditions using three representative packaging waste categories: plastic bottles, aluminium cans, and Tetra Pak containers. The SAM + MobileNetV2 perception pipeline achieved an accuracy of 0.93, precision of 0.93, recall of 0.92, and F1-score of 0.92. System-level experiments demonstrated successful integration of RGB-D object localization, conveyor tracking, camera-to-robot coordinate transformation, and robotic pick-and-place execution. In contrast to conventional high-throughput sorting systems, the proposed workstation emphasizes modularity, flexibility, and collaborative operation for small-batch industrial packaging waste streams. In addition, workstation-level manipulation tests over 200 grasp attempts resulted in a 92.0% grasp success rate, an 89.0% end-to-end sorting success rate, and an estimated sorting rate of 5.73 picks/min under controlled conveyor-based conditions. Discussion The results demonstrate the feasibility of integrating foundation-model-based perception with collaborative robot in a modular workstation intended for small-batch industrial packaging waste sorting. The proposed approach emphasizes flexibility, modularity, and reduced reconfiguration effort for variable waste streams. The results provide a basis for further development toward adaptive and human–robot collaborative sorting, while broader validation under more diverse, cluttered, and industrially representative conditions remains necessary.

Abstract Low‐stakes assessments are particularly vulnerable to rapid guessing behavior, where responses may reflect minimal cognitive engagement, potentially biasing scores and weakening inferences. Drawing on a scoping review of more than 70 studies, we summarize how rapid guessing is identified, its impact on key parameters, and how it is treated. Detection methods range from time‐based thresholds to statistical models using response‐time or residual data, each balancing practicality and precision. Treatments include filtering, downweighting, and model‐based adjustments, with differing consequences for score meaning and comparability. However, decisions about identifying rapid guessing, evaluating its impact, and selecting treatments are often not explicitly linked, making it difficult to arrive at coherent analytic choices. To address this, we propose a four‐step workflow and reporting guidelines: (1) clarify construct relevance, (2) screen using context‐appropriate methods, (3) assess impact via sensitivity analysis, and (4) justify a treatment. Together, these tools provide a practical framework for defensible educational measurement practice.

In human–robot collaboration, there are different levels of interaction. At lower levels, collisions must be avoided. At a higher level, collaborative robots directly interact with humans, and human health and safety need to be assured when designing work systems with robots included. In the process, adequate models of human motions are required. The diversity of human motions has led to ongoing research activities that have provided a considerable range of models. This chapter provides an overview of full-body human models such as kinematics, dynamics, and skin models and their applications in robotics. Kinematic models provide an abstraction of the human skeleton structure and its joints, whereas skin models provide mappings from the skeleton models to skin surfaces. Both are required for motion simulation with most human motion models. A survey of analytical, physics and data-driven human motion models is given. The state of the art as well as recent research advances are summarized for the models, and models of singular human motions and motion corridor/density models are differentiated. Their relevance for different levels of human–robot collaboration and ergonomics is discussed. Applications of motion models in the collaborative robotics domain and their respective advantages and shortcomings are reviewed with a special focus on their applicability for safety, efficiency and user experience in digital twins. Finally, the chapter presents three application scenarios in assembly lines and material handling in automotive industry.

Digital impressions and virtual patient technologies have become integral components of prosthodontic workflows linking clinical data acquisition, diagnosis, treatment planning, and restoration fabrication. This chapter aims to evaluate the technical foundations, clinical applications, accuracy, and limitations of intraoral scanning and virtual patient technologies in the context of the current literature. The optical principles of intraoral scanners, three-dimensional data acquisition, and file formats such as STL, PLY, and OBJ are outlined. Accuracy, trueness, and precision are distinguished, and the effects of scanning extent, scanning strategy, operator experience, preparation geometry, moisture control, and implant scan body characteristics on impression outcomes are considered. Indication-dependent applications of digital impressions in tooth-supported fixed restorations, implant-supported prostheses, and removable prosthodontics are compared with conventional techniques. Virtual patient construction is examined through the integration of intraoral scans, three-dimensional facial scans, cone-beam computed tomography, digital photographs, and mandibular motion records. Data registration, virtual articulators, digital facebows, and the transition from static three-dimensional models to dynamic four-dimensional representations are discussed. Although digital workflows may facilitate data exchange, visualization, and patient communication, full-arch and completely edentulous cases remain challenging because of recording accuracy, soft-tissue dynamics, interoperability, and costs. The potential of artificial intelligence-assisted design and individualized planning is considered alongside limitations in the available clinical evidence. Overall, digital impressions and virtual patient technologies should not be regarded as universal replacements for conventional procedures. Instead, they represent complementary tools whose use should be guided by clinical indication, required accuracy, patient-specific conditions, and available resources. The chapter emphasizes that technical feasibility alone does not establish clinical superiority and that careful validation is needed before emerging dynamic and artificial intelligence-based approaches are routinely implemented.

As undergraduate research increasingly relies on digital databases, analytical software, and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled technologies, research learning is potentially mediated through digital infrastructures that enable students to engage in knowledge construction. However, disparities in technological access and institutional support may constrain these learning opportunities. Guided by van Dijk’s digital divide model and Ragnedda’s concept of digital capital, this study employed interpretative phenomenological analysis (IPA) to examine how undergraduate students experienced digital readiness during the research process. Data were generated through three rounds of in-depth interviews with each of the eight undergraduate researchers at a Vietnamese public university. Analysis revealed that limited access to scholarly databases and research software usually restricted students’ engagement with technology-enhanced research learning. In addition, the absence of clear institutional policies and guidance regarding AI technologies potentially generated uncertainty about acceptable AI practices and contributed to uneven development of students’ digital competencies. These technological constraints influenced many students’ academic self-efficacy and reduced their ability to transform digital resources into meaningful learning and research outcomes. The effectiveness of technology-supported undergraduate research might depend not only on the availability of digital tools but also on equitable access, AI literacy development, and institutional support structures. The study contributes to the field of technologies in learning by demonstrating how digital infrastructure and technology governance may shape students’ participation in research-based learning. Implications are offered for the design of inclusive technology-enabled learning environments that support equitable undergraduate research engagement.

The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly transformed the landscape of digital storytelling, reshaping how narratives are created, shared, and experienced across various digital platforms. From automated content generation and interactive storytelling to virtual reality experiences and personalized narratives, AI has become an influential creative partner in media production, education, entertainment, journalism, marketing, and cultural preservation. This paper examines the evolving relationship between digital storytelling and artificial intelligence, focusing on how AI influences creativity, communication, and human experience. Using a qualitative review of existing literature, the study explores the historical evolution of storytelling, the emergence of AI-powered narrative systems, and the opportunities and challenges associated with AI-assisted creativity. The paper also discusses ethical concerns, including algorithmic bias, misinformation, copyright ownership, authenticity, and the changing role of human creators. Findings suggest that while AI enhances efficiency, personalization, and audience engagement, human imagination, emotional intelligence, cultural awareness, and ethical judgment remain indispensable components of meaningful storytelling. The study concludes that the future of storytelling lies in collaborative intelligence, where humans and AI work together to produce innovative, inclusive, and emotionally resonant narratives.

Digital technologies enable businesses to secure and manage information, which can be accessed at any time, allowing authorised users to make decisions more efficiently. Despite this potential, many SMEs in Nigeria are unable to fully maximise digital technologies, which limits their operational efficiency and competitiveness. This paper examined the impact of digital technologies on operational efficiency of SMEs in Lagos State, Nigeria, using a quantitative survey research design. A structured questionnaire was used to collect data from 166 SME owners, and both stratified and purposive sampling techniques were employed. Data were analysed using descriptive and inferential-regression analyses, while the paper was anchored on the technology acceptance and diffusion of innovation theories. The findings indicate that artificial intelligence and cloud computing play significant roles in product forecasting and improving business processes, but do not significantly contribute to inventory management. The paper further reveals that the effects of digital technologies are situational, requiring appropriate system integration, personnel capacity building, and alignment of operational processes. These findings can guide Lagos State SME managers and policymakers in enhancing efficiency, competitiveness, and sustainable business development.

Digital transformation in orthodontics refers to the digitization of patients’ clinical, photographic, radiological, and surface data; the integration of these data within a common digital environment; and the management of the workflow from diagnosis to retention based on these data. Intraoral scanners, digital models, cone-beam computed tomography, three-dimensional cephalometry, virtual treatment setups, clear aligner systems, artificial intelligence, and remote monitoring platforms contribute to making orthodontic decisions more measurable, reproducible, and shareable. Nevertheless, it should be recognized that digital tools do not inherently guarantee clinical success and that data quality, biological boundaries, operator supervision, and the sequencing of multidisciplinary treatment are decisive determinants of outcomes. This chapter addresses digital diagnostic and record-taking methods in orthodontics, intraoral scanning, three-dimensional and artificial intelligence-assisted cephalometric assessment, digital treatment planning, clear aligner workflows, and teleorthodontics. In addition, decision-making and treatment sequencing are discussed in multidisciplinary clinical situations involving impacted teeth, endodontically treated teeth, patients with periodontal problems, missing teeth, and orthodontic preparation before prosthetic treatment. The monitoring of biological risks, particularly root resorption, using digital data; the limitations of digital orthodontics; and the future transition toward personalized treatment models are also evaluated. The fundamental approach is to use digital technology not as a substitute for clinical examination, but as a decision-support system that addresses the appropriate clinical question and strengthens communication among specialists.

The governance of digital transformation in urban mobility presents defining policy challenges of contemporary urbanization. chapter critically re-examines the conceptual, empirical, and normative foundations of mobility scholarship by engaging, extending, and interrogating sources. The 21st century has witnessed a profound digital transformation across industries, influencing how societies function and how individuals interact with technology. original argument: smart mobility is fundamentally a governance contest rather than a technical challenge; dominant adoption frameworks require supplementation with platform economics and data justice theory; global electromobility disparities are structurally reproduced through financial and colonial data regimes; and algorithmic decision-making constitutes a governance frontier for which accountability mechanisms remain inadequate.chapter introduces the Sociotechnical Governance of Mobility framework organized around Technological, Institutional, domains, identifies research gaps, and proposes a democratic policy agenda for urban mobility

Abstract The chapter analyses the digitalisation of border controls as a means of preventive immigration control by focusing on the EUROSUR system of situational awareness based within Frontex and on the two key preventive EU immigration control databases: the Visa Information System (VIS) and the European Travel Information and Authorisation System (ETIAS). The analysis also focuses on calls for the interoperability of immigration databases and information systems in EU law, demonstrating their interconnections. The fundamental rights and rule of law implications of the digitalisation of the border are fully explored, including the impact on data protection and the challenges arising from the use of artificial intelligence.

Digitalization has become an important factor influencing economic growth, productivity, employment, innovation and the structural transformation of economies. The expansion of broadband networks, cloud computing, digital platforms, artificial intelligence, big data analytics, digital financial services and other information and communication technologies has changed the organization of production and the allocation of economic resources. This article examines the mechanisms through which digitalization contributes to economic growth and structural transformation, with particular attention to productivity, innovation, sectoral reallocation, labor markets, trade and the development of digital services. The study is based on a review and comparative analysis of evidence from the World Bank, OECD, International Telecommunication Union, UN Trade and Development and peer-reviewed academic literature. The evidence indicates that digital technologies can increase productivity by reducing transaction costs, improving information flows, facilitating automation, supporting innovation and expanding access to markets. However, the economic effects of digitalization are not automatic. Productivity gains depend on complementary investments in human capital, organizational capabilities, physical and digital infrastructure, competition and institutional quality. Digitalization can also contribute to structural transformation by facilitating the movement of economic activity toward higher-productivity manufacturing and service activities and by creating new digitally enabled occupations and business models. At the same time, differences in connectivity, affordability, digital skills and access to capital can cause the benefits of digital transformation to be distributed unevenly. The article concludes that digitalization should be treated not simply as technological modernization but as a broad economic transformation requiring coordinated policies in infrastructure, skills, innovation, competition and data governance.

As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) becomes increasingly integrated into education, understanding whether students possess the foundational conditions needed to benefit from AI-mediated learning has become an important educational challenge. This study conceptualizes dispositional foundations for AI-mediated learning as the configuration of ICT self-efficacy, attitudes toward technology and expectations of future ICT use that may support meaningful engagement with AI-mediated learning environments, and examines how these configurations relate to objectively assessed digital competence and to student characteristics. ICILS 2023 contains no measure of AI literacy or AI use, so these are candidate foundations rather than a direct measure of preparedness for AI. Using data from 118,764 Grade-8 students across 35 education systems participating in the International Computer and Information Literacy Study (ICILS 2023), we conducted sampling-weighted latent profile analyses on four internationally comparable indicators. Computer and information literacy (CIL) was examined as an external criterion using the BCH approach, and profile membership was predicted by socioeconomic background, gender, educational aspirations and ICT access. Four profiles emerged: average (55.9%), attitude-oriented (25.2%), low-disposition (11.0%) and efficacy-dominant (7.9%). Differences in CIL across profiles were modest, and students in the efficacy-dominant profile, who reported ICT self-efficacy more than two standard deviations above the mean, did not outperform the average profile in objectively assessed competence, a pattern we interpret as a confidence-competence mismatch rather than as high preparedness. On a common metric of average marginal effects, gender showed larger and more consistent contrasts than socioeconomic background. These findings suggest that the dispositional foundations for AI-mediated learning are distinct from computer and information literacy and should be understood as a multidimensional configuration of learner characteristics whose relevance to actual AI-mediated learning remains to be tested directly.

Abstract Accurate machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have made first-principles-quality potential energy surfaces increasingly accessible for condensed-phase chemistry, but their inference cost can still limit the sampling needed to compute experimentally relevant observables. In this work, we use knowledge distillation to construct compact “student” models that retain the accuracy of much larger “teacher” models obtained through either finetuning of foundation models or Δ-learning. The resulting students reduce production simulation cost by approximately an order of magnitude, making high-accuracy sampling practical for challenging condensed-phase problems. We demonstrate this across three problems of increasing sampling complexity: finite-temperature NPT simulations of ice Ih, classical and path-integral simulations of liquid water over 240–370 K, and path-integral umbrella-sampling simulations of water dissociation at the anatase TiO2(101)/water interface. When compared, the distilled students reproduce the target observables of their teachers more reliably than equally compact models trained only on the available reference data. The liquid water student, distilled from a Δ-learned CCSD(T)-quality teacher, reproduces thermodynamic, structural, transport, and nuclear quantum effects over the full temperature range studied. At the TiO2/water interface, knowledge distillation makes PIMD umbrella sampling practical and shows that nuclear quantum effects lower the dissociation barrier by approximately 2 kcal/mol and shift the molecular–dissociated free energy difference into closer agreement with recent solid-state 17O NMR measurements. Our work demonstrates how knowledge distillation can make accurate MLIPs practical for the sampling methods needed to connect condensed-phase reaction thermodynamics with experiment, notably for interfacial chemistry and catalysis.
topics: Advanced Physical and Chemical Molecular Interactions

documents.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to create digital advertising, but its effects on perceived sustainability communication remain unclear. This research examines whether AI authorship disclosure increases greenwashing suspicion and whether specific evidence-based claims mitigate this effect. Across three studies using promotional messages for a fictional sustainable delivery service, GreenDrop, we tested authorship disclosure, claim specificity, perceived authenticity, claim diagnosticity, visual attention, and physiological arousal. Study 1 showed that AI-labelled green advertisements elicited higher greenwashing suspicion and lower perceived authenticity than human-labelled advertisements, with a significant indirect association through perceived authenticity. Study 2 showed that specific evidence-based claims reduced greenwashing suspicion, increased claim diagnosticity, and attenuated—but did not eliminate—the AI-disclosure penalty. Study 3 replicated this interaction in a laboratory setting and added eye-tracking and GSR evidence: AI-labelled advertisements increased attention to the authorship label, specific claims altered visual allocation toward claim-related information, and AI-labelled vague claims elicited higher physiological arousal. Overall, AI disclosure operates as a source-attribution cue that can undermine authenticity and heighten greenwashing suspicion, especially when sustainability claims are vague.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Technology-mediated sexual behaviours, including cybersex and technosex, are becoming increasingly prevalent as digital technologies, virtual reality, artificial intelligence, and interactive devices continue to develop. Although these behaviours may offer numerous benefits, such as facilitating sexual exploration, supporting individuals with disabilities, and enabling long-distance intimacy, they may also contribute to problematic patterns of use in some individuals. This review synthesises current knowledge on the psychological and neurobiological mechanisms underlying cybersex and technosexual behaviour. The article discusses conceptual and definitional issues, epidemiological data, and theoretical frameworks, including the Triple A model and the “quasi-necrophilia” framework, to explain the characteristics and motivations behind technology-mediated sexual activities. Furthermore, it summarises psychological factors associated with both adaptive and maladaptive use, emphasising the role of emotion regulation, personality traits, neurodevelopmental conditions, mental health, and sexual motivations. The review also presents current evidence on the neurobiology of cybersex and technosex, highlighting the involvement of dopaminergic reward pathways and similarities to other reward-related behaviours. Finally, available approaches to the treatment of problematic technology-mediated sexual behaviour are discussed, including pharmacotherapy, as well as psychoeducation and psychotherapy, with particular attention to the importance of addressing underlying psychological conditions. The article argues that cybersex and technosex should not be inherently pathologised—instead, they should be understood within a biopsychosocial framework that distinguishes between healthy sexual expression and clinically significant impairment.

This exploratory case study examines the feasibility of integrating generative artificial intelligence (AI) into a low-cost Kundt’s tube activity in pre-service science teacher education. The proposed Do-It-With-AI framework comprises four phases: conceptual exploration, design development, troubleshooting, and extension to real-world applications. Scopus AI was used to support the literature-oriented conceptual exploration, while ChatGPT-4 and ChatGPT-5 supported the generation of design alternatives, troubleshooting hypotheses, and possible extensions. Three pre-service teachers constructed and tested the apparatus, and successive configurations were evaluated through resonance measurements and estimation of the speed of sound. The case illustrates how AI-generated suggestions can be incorporated into an iterative design–test–verification process in which proposed modifications are examined against physical principles and experimental evidence. The four-phase sequence is therefore presented as a feasible framework for integrating generative AI with hands-on experimentation, with instructor-guided verification serving as an essential component. Because the present study focuses on feasibility and process rather than educational outcomes, further investigation with larger cohorts and explicit measures of student reasoning, learning, collaboration, and AI literacy is required. The principal contribution of the Kundt’s tube case is to demonstrate a structured and empirically grounded use of generative AI in low-cost experimental development within pre-service science teacher education.

Generative AI is increasingly used in academic writing, although many studies compare only human-written and AI-generated text. This within-subjects study examined manual, AI-revised, and AI-generated extended abstracts in a graduate human factors course. Text analyses included 96 abstracts from 32 participants, and repeated-measures survey analyses included 30 participants. We compared structural and lexical features, readability, Sentence-BERT embeddings, exploratory writing-condition classification, technology acceptance, and perceived workload. Manual abstracts showed the greatest variability. AI-generated abstracts showed less structural variability, higher lexical density, and greater estimated reading difficulty. AI-revised abstracts showed metric-specific overlap with both other conditions. A three-class classifier yielded 68.75% accuracy under abstract-level leave-one-out cross-validation, although participant and topic overlap limits generalization. Participants reported greater acceptance and lower workload in the AI-supported conditions. These preliminary findings motivate examining degrees of AI involvement and using participant-grouped validation in future studies.

As LLMs become increasingly capable of implementing software, a critical bottleneck emerges: whether they truly understand what users want. Users often begin with vague intent, leaving important requirements to be clarified through interaction. In repository-level development, misunderstandings can propagate and cause costly rework. However, existing benchmarks typically evaluate implementation from complete specifications or underspecified requests, overlooking pre-coding requirement clarification. Prior clarification studies mainly focus on function-level tasks. It therefore remains unclear how well LLMs can transform vague intent into clear requirements through interaction and how this capability affects subsequent code generation. We introduce ReqClarifyBench, an interactive requirement clarification benchmark for repository-level software development. It contains 341 tasks spanning game, miniapp, and web development, each with a vague user intent, a human-validated requirement document, and code evaluation artifacts. We employ LLM-based user simulators with diverse personas derived from real-world conversations. We evaluate six LLMs in terms of clarification effectiveness and generated requirement document quality. Results show that stronger clarification effectiveness does not necessarily translate into higher document quality, and performance varies substantially across user personas. We also find that coding-agent harnesses do not further improve requirement document quality compared with their base LLMs. These findings offer insights for building LLM-based end-to-end software development systems.

LLM-as-a-Service has become a dominant paradigm for accessing large language models without requiring local deployment. However, the process raises severe privacy concerns when user queries may include sensitive or confidential contexts. Differential privacy (DP) provides a principled approach to protecting such inputs, but existing DP inference methods are primarily designed for short- or moderate-context settings and struggle with million-token-scale inputs due to limited context capacity and severe utility degradation under DP perturbation. In this paper, we propose DP-MIND, a memory-guided framework that scales differentially private inference to million-token contexts. DP-MIND enables private long-context inference by locally perturbing the input and processing it chunk by chunk with a compact memory that preserves task-relevant information across the sequence. To make this memory robust to DP noise, we optimize the memory construction policy directly on perturbed inputs using reinforcement learning, guided by both final answer correctness and memory consistency. We further recover perturbation-corrupted answer spans through a local denoising module without exposing the original context to the external model. We provide theoretical privacy analysis of DP-MIND and further conduct extensive empirical analysis across multiple long-context benchmarks with context lengths up to the million-token scale, demonstrating that DP-MIND consistently outperforms existing DP and long-context inference baselines in both scalability and utility.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in everyday teaching, yet its environmental costs remain largely absent from how educators reason about its use. This study examines how 22 teachers working in public schools in Türkiye, each with at least one academic year of experience integrating artificial intelligence into the classroom, interpret and navigate these technologies at the intersection of pedagogical effectiveness, professional responsibility, and ecological sustainability. Semi-structured interviews were analyzed through Braun and Clarke’s reflexive thematic analysis within a generic interpretive qualitative design. Five themes were developed. The first three show teachers actively mediating AI through pedagogical judgment, a restructured professional agency, and a renewed relational and epistemic role. The study’s central contribution lies in the final two: for almost all participants, AI’s ecological cost was not unknown but rendered invisible in everyday practice—a professionally produced ordering of attention enacted through the very pedagogical agency that makes teachers effective. When this cost surfaced, teachers managed rather than resolved the tension through pedagogical rationalization and self-reported intentions toward ecologically motivated restraint, while extending their moral concern to students’ cognitive dependence. Ecological invisibility thus emerges not as a knowledge deficit but as a by-product of professional attention—one that teacher education and policy should address through a critical AI literacy integrating ethical, ecological, and pedagogical dimensions.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Education has a long association with nation building, social change, and human development. Mahamana Pandit Madan Mohan Malaviya believed that education is necessary for the development of character, national consciousness, social responsibility and a self-reliant nation. The objective of his education was to bring together Indian cultural traditions with moral values and Indian spiritual ideals with modern science, technical knowledge, vocational competence and research. The institutionalisation of this vision was in the form of Banaras Hindu University, which aimed at integrating Indian knowledge traditions with modern education and professional training. This present study focuses on Malaviya's Educational Philosophy and its relevance in the present context in the National Education Policy 2020. The study is qualitative in nature and descriptive and analytical in design and relied entirely on secondary sources like the speeches and writings of Malaviya, institutional documents of BHU, National Education Policy 2020, Indian knowledge system guidelines and relevant academic literature. This analysis is based on five dimensions namely holistic and value-based education, education for nation-building, empowerment of teacher, skill and vocational education and integration of Indian Knowledge Systems with modern scientific knowledge. The study finds significant conceptual relevance of Malaviya’s educational ideas with NEP 2020. Both approaches view education as a way of building intellectually capable, ethically responsible, socially sensitive, culturally rooted and professionally competent citizens. Yet, Malaviya’s ideas should not be mechanically adopted. Its modern relevance requires a critical engagement with constitutional values, pluralism, scientific temper, digital transformation, artificial intelligence, social diversity and changing employment requirements. The paper concludes that Malaviya’s educational vision can provide an important philosophical basis for implementing NEP 2020 and developing an inclusive, innovative, self-reliant and socially responsible India.

Abstract Currently, machine learning technology has been widely used in electroencephalogram (EEG) automatic emotion recognition tasks. However, the non-stationarity, individual differences, and high annotation costs in EEG signals seriously affect the generalization ability of the model. To solve these problems, we propose a new unsupervised domain adaptation framework named EEG-UDAF for EEG emotion recognition. First, we design a dual-view frequency domain feature fusion module that can extract rich EEG signals frequency domain features from two perspectives, differential entropy and power spectral density, and fuse them based on the self-attention mechanism. Second, we propose a spatio-temporal feature extraction module based on graph convolutional network and bidirectional long short-term memory. It can comprehensively consider the spatial topological structure of the brain and the dynamic characteristics of temporal changes between EEG channels to extract complex spatio-temporal features. Third, we use the unsupervised domain adaptation strategy to solve the non-stationarity and individual differences in EEG signals without manual annotation, and introduce a semantic correction mechanism to prevent incorrect class alignment. Experiments based on intra-subject and inter-subject paradigms show that EEG-UDAF can effectively alleviate non-stationarity and individual differences. Moreover, these transferable EEG representations also provide a potential foundation for LLM-augmented multimodal data fusion in large-scale affective computing.

Choking under pressure refers to suboptimal performance under stressful conditions in an individual who, based on prior performance, would be expected to perform at a higher level. Although most observed in sports, choking can occur in musical performance, test-taking, and other skilled domains. The present study used typing to examine the effects of monitoring pressure, outcome pressure, and task difficulty on the cognitive processes underlying typing. Seventy-six undergraduates were randomly assigned to one of four between-subjects conditions: control, monitoring pressure (video camera), outcome pressure (monetary competition), or combined pressure. Participants copy-typed high- and low-frequency four-letter words; reaction time to first keystroke (RT1), inter-keystroke interval (IKSI), and error rate indexed outer-loop, inner-loop, and accuracy processes respectively. Results revealed no evidence of choking under any pressure condition, but consistent task difficulty effects: low-frequency words slowed both RT1 and IKSI. These findings suggest typing is resilient to moderate pressure and highlight its promise as an accessible testbed for choking research.

Background University students experience substantial mental-health burdens, while access to timely support remains uneven. AI conversational agents may provide low-threshold support, but the evidence base has expanded rapidly and prior reviews have often combined different age groups, intervention types, outcome domains, and comparator conditions. Objective To evaluate the effects of AI-mediated conversational interventions on depressive and anxiety symptoms in university students, while distinguishing outcome domains, comparator intensity, intervention architecture, and the evidential requirements for standardized post-intervention effect estimation. Methods We updated the search in PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, CENTRAL, and Web of Science to the revised search date and rebuilt an auditable cross-database record ledger. The updated workflow included 3,786 exported records, 451 DOI/PMID duplicates, 41 confirmed title/author duplicates, and 3,294 unique records screened. All title/abstract records completed a two-reviewer screening and consensus chain. Forty-six update-search records entered research-level/full-text assessment. Randomized controlled trials were eligible for causal quantitative synthesis; relevant feasibility, acceptability, usability, and non-comparable controlled studies were retained narratively. Standard post-intervention analyses used Hedges g, REML random-effects models, and Hartung-Knapp adjustment, and were restricted to attributable two-group post-intervention data. Results In the final locked non-active/low-intensity comparator analysis, three depression comparisons favored conversational interventions (k=3; Hedges g=-0.413, 95% CI -0.557 to -0.268; I2 = 0.0%) and four anxiety comparisons also favored them (k=4; Hedges g=-0.435, 95% CI -0.603 to -0.268; I2 = 2.1%). In the separate active conversational-control analysis, two MYLO comparisons did not show a reliable incremental effect for depression (k=2; g=0.165, 95% CI -0.580 to 0.911) or anxiety (k=2; g=0.190, 95% CI -0.556 to 0.937). The evidence base remained small, clinically heterogeneous, and limited by attrition, self-reported outcomes, and uncertainty regarding generalizability. Conclusions AI conversational interventions may improve depressive and anxiety symptoms relative to non-active or low-intensity comparators in university students, but the certainty of evidence is low and estimates are based on few comparisons. Evidence against active conversational controls is very uncertain. Outcome-domain differences and architecture-related claims should be treated as hypothesis-generating. Secure, consent-based, human-supervised implementation and objective outcome assessment are priorities for future research. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261323382 , identifier CRD420261323382.
topics: Anxiety, Depression, Psychometrics, Treatment, Cognitive Processes

documents.abstract: Metaverse, a virtual shared space, is a promising avenue for transforming supply chain operations through emerging trends and technologies shaping the future of suppliers, manufacturers, retailers, and customers. This chapter examines the emerging trends and technologies that are shaping the future of the supply chain metaverse. Emerging trends include advanced virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and digital twins, which are creating immersive and interactive spaces for stakeholders to interact with digital representations of supply chain operations. Artificial intelligence and machine learning provide data-driven optimization, and the metaverse can be used to simulate different scenarios, test new solutions, and optimize processes based on real-time data analysis. Additionally, blockchain ensures secure, transparent record-keeping for product provenance, reducing fraud and improving compliance. Furthermore, this chapter provides practical scenarios on how the supply chain metaverse can improve transparency and increase agility. Finally, this chapter concludes by acknowledging the need for interdisciplinary research and collaboration to address the challenges and unlock the full potential of the supply chain metaverse.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: In many segmentation approaches, customer identity and purchase behaviour are emphasised, while the emotional experience of the customer–brand relationship is often overlooked. This conceptual paper proposes the Emotion-Centric Customer Segmentation and Loyalty (ECSL) framework for the generative AI era, linking emotional foundations (emotions, attachment, and perceived experience quality) to emotion-centric segmentation and AI-enabled interaction fit (tone, offers, service scripts, and journey orchestration). AI and generative AI are positioned as enablers that help sense emotional cues and support segment-fit responses across touchpoints. Value co-creation behaviours and loyalty outcomes (retention, commitment, advocacy) are presented as downstream results, while ethical governance and trust (transparency, consent, fairness, accountability, and human oversight) are treated as essential conditions that strengthen or weaken these effects. Directions are outlined for future empirical testing of the model and its moderation mechanisms.

As generative AI chatbots increasingly serve as emotional companions, understanding their implications for users’ emotional and social lives is critical. This 14-day diary study involving 97 social chatbot users examined how daily loneliness relates to chatbot engagement and subsequent psychosocial outcomes. Bayesian multilevel models showed that on days when participants felt lonelier than usual, they reported longer chatbot use and stronger emotional engagement. Notably, these two forms of engagement showed distinct associations with daily outcomes. Emotional engagement was associated with higher daily subjective well-being but shorter interpersonal interaction duration, whereas longer usage duration was associated with lower interpersonal interaction pleasure. Mediation analyses reflected the same patterns. These findings highlight the importance of distinguishing behavioral from emotional engagement with social chatbots and suggest that emotional benefits and interpersonal costs may coexist in everyday human–AI interaction, informing the responsible design and balanced use of social AI companions.

Introduction Emotional design integrates sensory, functional, social, and symbolic elements to elicit affective responses that may influence consumer perception, attitudes, and behavior. This study aimed to analyze the relationship between emotional design, advertising, and consumer behavior based on recent scientific literature. Methods A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA guidelines. Searches were performed in Scopus and Web of Science, and 66 primary studies published during the last ten years were included. Results The reviewed evidence shows that emotional design strategies incorporate perceptual stimuli, user experiences, and meaning-making processes. Color, shape, texture, packaging, and multisensory stimuli contribute to attraction, attention, and perceived quality, while usability, ergonomics, interactivity, and demonstrations enhance the user experience. Storytelling, cultural identity, sustainability, and personalization contribute to meaning construction and strengthen consumer-brand connections. The literature also identifies positive, negative, and complex emotions, including pleasure, trust, fear, guilt, nostalgia, attachment, and identification, which are associated with purchase intention, satisfaction, loyalty, repurchase, and other consumer responses. Discussion The findings indicate that emotional design operates across sensory, experiential, social, and symbolic dimensions, extending its influence beyond immediate purchase decisions toward longer-term consumer-brand relationships. However, the methodological diversity of the reviewed studies highlights the need for more integrated approaches combining subjective, physiological, and digital measures to evaluate emotional and behavioral responses. documents.abstract: This chapter examines the integration of emotional intelligence and neuroadaptive leadership in hospitality management. As hospitality organizations face technological transformation, workforce diversity, evolving customer expectations, and increasing uncertainty, effective leadership requires emotional and cognitive adaptability. The chapter reviews emotional intelligence, neuroleadership, adaptive leadership, and organizational neuroscience literature to propose a conceptual framework linking self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy, and social skills with cognitive flexibility, learning agility, resilience, situational awareness, and adaptive decision-making. The framework explains how these capabilities influence employee engagement, service quality, guest satisfaction, organizational resilience, and organizational performance. Practical implications and future research directions are discussed. The chapter demonstrates that emotional intelligence provides the foundation for neuroadaptive leadership and sustainable success in hospitality organizations.

This paper offers a theory-informed commentary on the executive-employee gap in enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) readiness, using a CIO.com feature on employee AI optimism and an AI leadership gap as its focal practitioner text. Rather than treating the article as empirical evidence, the paper interprets it through scholarship on socio-technical change, organizational readiness, AI governance, work design, and incentive alignment, using 2024-2025 industry reports as context. It examines how the text frames the readiness gap, how socio-technical and incentive-alignment perspectives explain it, and what operational risks may follow. The analysis suggests the leadership gap is better understood as an organizational-design problem than as employee resistance or a training deficit. When AI tools are introduced without changes to workflows, governance, learning, and accountability, employees may face burdens and uncertainty about legitimate AI use. The paper contributes by framing AI readiness as an organizational condition, integrating socio-technical and incentive-alignment perspectives, identifying shadow AI, weak output validation, data-quality problems, and accountability ambiguity as risk pathways, and proposing a Socio-Technical AI Readiness Framework linking AI pressure, readiness architecture, employee readiness, operational transformation, and risk leakage. For managers, sustainable AI transformation requires credible organizational conditions for AI-enabled work, not merely greater tool use.

The metaverse has emerged as a transformative virtual environment where individuals interact digitally, offering significant potential for supply chain operations through real-time tracking capabilities. This technological evolution has enhanced business efficiency by reducing costs and improving transparency across multiple operational levels. By combining augmented reality, virtual reality, and artificial intelligence, the metaverse creates immersive, interactive spaces for work, training, and collaboration. This chapter examines how metaverse technologies are revolutionizing human resource functions—particularly workforce training and skill development within supply chain management. It investigates how the metaverse establishes innovative learning environments that transform workforce development in logistics, warehouse management, and related fields. Using a qualitative research methodology, this work comprehensively reviews the existing literature to understand connections between metaverse applications and supply chain workforce skill enhancement. The research includes case analyses of organizations that have implemented metaverse-based training in their supply chain operations. This chapter incorporates perspectives from industry professionals regarding metaverse training adoption processes, implementation challenges, and effectiveness metrics. Research findings strongly indicate that metaverse-driven training and skill development initiatives have substantially improved workforce efficiency and enhanced employee knowledge retention. However, this chapter also addresses significant challenges, including high infrastructure costs, shortages of qualified trainers, and ethical considerations.

Background Public-sector information institutions operate amid continuous change, rising service demands, and complex tasks. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources and Conservation of Resources perspectives, this study examines whether workplace spirituality functions as a motivational resource linking job characteristics, transformational leadership, and coworker incivility to innovative work behavior (IWB) among information professionals. Method A cross-sectional survey was conducted with 150 employees of Indonesian public libraries (n = 93) and archives (n = 57). Hypotheses were tested with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), including assessment of discriminant validity (Fornell–Larcker, HTMT), collinearity (VIF), effect sizes (f 2 ), predictive relevance (Q 2 ), and model fit (SRMR). Result Workplace spirituality showed the strongest association with IWB (β = 0.652) and accounted for a substantial share of the associations of job characteristics (indirect β = 0.437) and transformational leadership (indirect β = 0.093) with IWB, indicating complementary partial mediation rather than full mediation. The total effect of coworker incivility on IWB was not significant (β = 0.105); its association operated indirectly through workplace spirituality (β = −0.078). The model explained 63.0% of the variance in workplace spirituality and 68.5% in IWB, with predictive relevance established (Q 2 = 0.325 and 0.434). These patterns are consistent with a model in which structural and interpersonal work conditions relate to innovation largely — though not exclusively — through employees’ experienced meaning, community, and value congruence, although the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. Conclusion The findings suggest that cultivating workplace spirituality (meaningful work, sense of community, value alignment), enriching job design, and curbing coworker incivility may support innovation in public libraries and archives. Generalization to galleries and museums awaits further research.

Artificial intelligence is beginning to automate scientific discovery, yet physical robot-policy research still relies on scientists and engineers to interpret experimental failures and decide how controllers should be revised. We present EndoRSI (Endoscopic Recursive Self-Improvement), a human-governed, self-improving robotic research system in which the embedded EndoForge coding agent iteratively develops and refines endoscopic robot policies using evidence from physical experiments. Physical execution remains isolated within a safety-constrained runtime under human authorisation. In motorised endoscopy, validation evidence first caused the agent to reject an initial action representation, while subsequent physical experiments falsified an offline-supported insertion strategy by revealing hazardous closed-loop behaviour absent from the source data. Failed physical rollouts were then incorporated into policy revision; insertion success subsequently increased from 2/21 in the first generation to 17/21 in the fourth. The frozen final policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and was the best performing autonomous policy across six independent ex-vivo porcine specimens. These results show that physical robot interaction can serve as experimental evidence for agent-driven robot policy research.

Some of the toughest problems corporations, organizations, and societies face are wicked problems. Conventional or “tame” problems have right answers and best choices that can be determined using analytical methods. In contrast, wicked problems ( Rittel & Webber, 1973 ) are impossible to solve definitively but can only be managed because they are big, messy, laden with unintended consequences, and filled with conflict between stakeholders who have multiple competing interests. Analytical methods designed for conventional problems won’t work effectively against problems like illegal drugs, societal inequality, poverty, debt, war, or homelessness. We conducted an investigation of 32 actual wicked or near-wicked problems to identify practices that seemed effective and those that failed to work or even got in the way of progress. We found that progress depended on revising goals, aligning the goals of multiple stakeholders, and reframing the way the situation is understood. From this investigation, we formulated a set of recommendations. These include judging whether a problem is wicked, and if so shifting mindset to a flexible perspective, and making use of relevant tools, along with mistakes to avoid. We also suggest a potentially positive perspective on wicked problems—that in some situations they can support change and adaptation rather than rigidity and conformity.

This chapter examines the transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in reshaping Entrepreneurial Education (EE) for non-WEIRD—-Western, Educated, Industrialised, Rich, and Democratic—countries. Beginning with the foundational critique of WEIRD samples in social and behavioural science, and extending the recent roadmap for non-WEIRD entrepreneurship research, this chapter argues that the most urgent and under-theorised challenge in the global EE literature is not the integration of AI per se, but the contextual adaptation of AI-enabled pedagogies to the specific socio-economic, linguistic, infrastructural, and institutional realities of non-WEIRD national settings. To address this challenge, the chapter proposes the AI-EENI framework—AI-Enabled Entrepreneurial Education for Non-WEIRD Inclusion. The framework is a six-layer predictive-prescriptive model that leverages internationally validated secondary datasets and AI forecasting methodologies to generate actionable EE interventions without the requirement for primary data collection in fragile or resource-constrained contexts. The AI-EENI framework integrates DARQ+ technologies—Distributed ledger, AI, Reality technologies, and Quantum computing—into a coherent, contextually sensitive architecture for non-WEIRD EE delivery. This framework is applied to Ghana as practical evidence. The chapter contributes to the growing literature on AI in education, non-WEIRD entrepreneurship, and responsible technology deployment, whilst offering practical prescriptions for educators, policymakers, and international development agencies working towards SDG 4.

Purpose This study aims to reexamine Schumpeter’s framework of entrepreneurship and creative destruction to assess its explanatory power in artificial intelligence (AI)-intensive capitalism, where algorithmic technologies reshape the structural conditions under which entrepreneurial agency and innovation unfold. Design/methodology/approach This study adopted a conceptual reinterpretation approach grounded in a close reading of Schumpeter’s principal texts, placing this reconstruction in dialogue with contemporary literature on AI and entrepreneurship, as well as with post-Schumpeterian patterns, including Schumpeter Mark I, Mark II and intellectual monopoly dynamics. Findings Moreover, AI confirmed the Schumpeterian conceptual core, radicalised its dynamics through temporal compression and ecosystemic displacement and necessitated a partial reformulation. Entrepreneurial judgement under radical uncertainty remained irreducible, although agency became distributed across hybrid human-algorithmic configurations where formative creativity grows increasingly automatable, while transformative creativity was dependent on human judgement. Creative destruction shifts towards platform-governed ecosystemic architectures and the prevailing Schumpeterian pattern depends on each sector’s appropriability and governance conditions, rather than on the technology itself. Where intellectual monopoly dynamics prevail, innovation is co-produced across the periphery and the capture of its returns concentrates asymmetrically at the nucleus. Originality/value This study rethinks the relationship between entrepreneurship, creative destruction and AI by reinterpreting the internal tensions in Schumpeter’s work. Based on this reconstruction, it develops a framework of distributed agency and ecosystemic creative destruction centred on the distinction between formative and transformative creativity at the institutional level and identifies the appropriate conditions under which innovation generates structural discontinuities. This further shows that the Schumpeterian patterns associated with AI emerge from sector-specific configurations of appropriability and governance, providing a structural explanation that previous management literature had left underdeveloped.

Ergonomics is inherently based on disciplinary integration: a compulsory condition to lead the systemic understanding and improvement of real-world complexities like the ones of Human-Robot Interactions (HRIs). Accordingly, this chapter ponders the contributions of diverse disciplines to the study of human factors alongside their synergies with the multi-faceted area of robotics. Key examples are presented, considering problems requiring approaches like bio-inspired soft robotics, value-sensitive design, interactions and affective features, and neuroergonomics in HRI. The implications about education on HRI ergonomics are also pondered. Overall, this chapter remarks how diverse backgrounds can lead to contributions to the human-centered design and assessment of robots if the experts, regardless of disciplinary boundaries, just focus on learning novel perspectives and methods to solve the problems occurring in Human-Robot Systems.

The development, implementation and use of technological artifacts introduces ethical issues—technologies are not ethically neutral. This ethical dimension is particularly obvious in robotic technologies, as many types and applications of robots are situated at the intersection of automation and social interaction. Consequently, developers, researchers and users of robots are confronted with ethical issues, for example concerning safety or (human) autonomy. With respect to ergonomics, two main themes can be identified: (1) Ergonomics itself involves certain values such as well-being, accessibility, performance optimization, safety, and trust. These values (and others) can and should be discussed in ethical terms. (2) Complex ethical issues in human–robot interaction are often difficult to address and can be cognitively overwhelming in the design process. One common ad-hoc strategy is to simply bypass and ignore these potential issues. However, professional tools that deal with ethical issues in the development and use of robotic system are available and may help to advance values in robotics. The most widely acknowledged framework to address values embedded in socio-technical systems during the development process is Value Sensitive Design (VSD). Focusing on ethical values, we present this framework with respect to robotic technologies. Finally, as implied by the very idea of human–robot interaction, robots themselves can be interpreted as subjects of action. This interpretation suggests an ethical reflection of the actions and behaviors performed by robots as if they were moral agents, an idea that is at odds with the key themes of ergonomics, values and ethics of robotics.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This cross-sectional study examined how MBA students appraise ethical concerns, practical benefits, social expectations, control, and institutional governance related to educational artificial intelligence (AI). The analysis used 275 eligible responses submitted by the prespecified study cut-off. Descriptive statistics, omega and Spearman-Brown reliability, exploratory factor analysis (EFA), rank-based and bootstrap robustness checks, and regression models of ordered AI experience were used. Three exploratory dimensions were retained in 90.4% of 500 bootstrap samples. A proportional-odds reference model improved on the null model, chi-square(6) = 17.81, p = .007, but the proportional-odds assumption was rejected, chi-square(6) = 17.81, p = .007; threshold-specific models were therefore primary. AI self-efficacy/control was associated with reporting at least moderate rather than none/minimal AI experience (OR = 1.51, 95% CI [1.13, 2.03], p = .005), and this result persisted after background adjustment, bootstrap validation, and response-quality screens. In the smaller extensive-experience comparison (n = 26), efficiency benefit and perceived ethical-issue frequency were positive exploratory correlates. Concern was highest for data privacy, while governance responses indicated comparatively limited knowledge of personal-data practices. Predictive performance was modest. The findings support clearer task-specific guidance, critical AI literacy, and transparent data practices, but the cross-sectional self-report design does not establish causal adoption effects or validated moral profiles.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Background As generative AI becomes increasingly embedded in higher education, it presents significant challenges related to ethical use, academic integrity and students' potential over‐reliance on AI‐generated outputs. The Think Aloud method offers a pedagogical approach for making students' reasoning visible as they interact with generative AI tools. Objective This mixed‐methods action research study explored the role of the Think Aloud method as a pedagogical intervention in supporting students' metacognitive awareness and ethical engagement with generative AI tools in a first‐year entrepreneurship course. Method Data were collected through reflective journals, classroom observations and a post‐intervention survey. The study involved 44 first‐year undergraduate students, with 38 students completing the post‐intervention survey. Qualitative data were analysed thematically, while survey responses were examined using descriptive statistics and an exploratory correlation analysis. Results and Conclusions Findings suggested that Think Aloud supported students' emerging awareness of prompt construction, verification practices and ethical decision‐making when using generative AI. However, students' critical evaluation of AI‐generated content often remained at a surface level, particularly among students requiring additional support. The study indicates that Think Aloud can make students' AI‐related reasoning more visible and can support more intentional engagement with generative AI, but it should not be viewed as a stand‐alone solution. Rather, it appears most effective when embedded within a broader pedagogical framework that includes AI literacy, prompt engineering, verification strategies and evaluative judgement. The study contributes classroom‐based evidence on process‐oriented approaches to ethical generative AI use in higher education and highlights the need for sustained instructional scaffolding to support deeper critical engagement with AI tools.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This abstract discuss how neuromarketing and generative AI converge to allow hyper-personalized emotional branding. It suggests the Ethical Adaptive Emotional Narrative Framework, a theoretical concept that brings in emotional data analysis, AI-generated marketing content, and is in line with the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. The framework categorizes emotionally adaptive marketing into four processes that are data capture, emotion inference, generative content adaptation and feedback learning. Every stage includes protection mechanisms, like approval, transparency, proportionality, and human control, to avoid manipulation and ensure the freedom of consumers. The chapter, by introducing the principle of emotional integrity, shows how organizations can use emotionally responsive AI systems to engage and build trust and yet remain ethically accountable and compliant with regulations.
