documents.abstract: Abstract Traditional terminology standards often assume that trained users can resolve coexisting translation variants through contextual judgement. As generative artificial intelligence (genAI) and large language models (LLMs) increasingly mediate terminology reuse, this raises questions about whether standards encode sufficiently explicit term-selection information for auditable automated selection. This study uses ChatGPT-4o in a prompt-testing procedure to examine whether the WHO’s 2007 and 2022 Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) terminology standards provide sufficient guidance for AI-mediated selection among coexisting English variants. Each sampled term was tested using the same three-prompt sequence: constrained variant selection, brief justification, and a within-session shift from general medical use to possible use in a WHO terminology standard. The model consistently followed the single-choice restriction. Its rationales clustered into four observable justification patterns. Most responses to the third prompt stated that the initial choice would remain unchanged; these responses are reported only as statements produced under this specific sequence. The findings suggest that terminology standards designed for human readability may not provide sufficiently explicit guidance for AI-mediated variant selection. The study therefore proposes a governance stress-test procedure and a minimal set of candidate executable fields for term selection, subject to expert validation and controlled testing.

From Repositories to Knowledge Ecosystems : Artificial Intelligence, Open Science and Adaptive Library Spaces in Indian Higher Education Dr. Amar Nath* Indian academic libraries are undergoing a significant transformation from collection-centred repositories into digitally connected knowledge ecosystems. This transformation is being shaped by the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020, expanding national digital infrastructures, artificial intelligence (AI), open-science practices, and changing expectations of learners and researchers. This study examines the emerging knowledge-ecosystem model in Indian higher education through documentary research and secondary-data analysis based on government policies, national digital platforms, institutional reports, and recent scholarly literature. Particular attention is given to three interrelated dimensions: AI-enabled discovery and intelligent library services, open-science infrastructure and scholarly access, and adaptive physical and hybrid learning spaces. The analysis focuses on national initiatives including One Nation One Subscription (ONOS), Shodhganga, the National Digital Library of India (NDLI), and VIDWAN. The official ONOS platform reports more than 6,500 member institutions and more than 1,140 lakh full-text downloads during 2025. Shodhganga crossed the milestone of 600,000 theses in May 2025, while VIDWAN currently reports more than 3.38 lakh academic peers in its verified research directory. These developments demonstrate the increasing importance of interoperable digital infrastructure in supporting research, discovery, collaboration, and lifelong learning. However, technological expansion is accompanied by challenges involving digital inequality, professional competencies, infrastructure, privacy, algorithmic bias, intellectual property, and uneven institutional capacity. The paper proposes a four-layer knowledge-ecosystem framework comprising infrastructure and connectivity; AI and knowledge processing; user-centred services and adaptive spaces; and governance, ethics and professional capacity. The paper argues that the future-ready academic library should no longer be conceptualised merely as a repository of information resources but as an integrated knowledge infrastructure connecting people, content, technology, research, learning and scholarly communication. * Post Graduate Government College, Sector-11, Chandigarh

The literature review of the paper on job crafting and subjective well-being relies on bibliometric analysis. The key conclusions are that such categories like Commerce, Management, Human Resources and Industry, Tourism and Services, and Human Society and Psychology prevail. There are evident conceptual clusters, e.g. work engagement and job resources-demands and emerging themes such as well-being in digital and educational environment. The review shows the fast field development and identifies the future research directions that would include digital work settings, cross-cultural research, and long-term research. The existing knowledge can assist the researchers and practitioners in enhancing the employee welfare and attaining sustainable organizational performance. Although there is literature on narrative and empirical research, there has been a dearth of systematic mapping, yet this review identifies the growth of job crafting and well-being research into fields of education, health sciences and information systems. The future research directions are multi-region studies, the significance of digital transformation, and sustainable work design. On the whole, it is possible to note that the given review presents the current knowledge and focuses on digital work environments, cross-cultural viewpoints, and longitudinal approaches to the issue. Its results are relevant to management practice in addressing the contemporary workplace issues.

This article investigates and explores the prototype of a material based project generation system, aiming to transform online DIY content into structured design knowledge for sustainable reuse. Based on an unfinished system developed by the author in his early years, this work reviews the methods of collecting unstructured data from the Internet, extracts key information through lightweight natural language processing, and normalizes it into a unified model suitable for automatic generation. Discussed baseline strategies for retrieving and editing project generation, as well as evaluation metrics that consider constraint satisfaction, feasibility, and user experience. The paper also investigates practical applications in personal creativity support, maker education, and community recycling, supported by initial human in the loop implementation and interactive segmentation code that links material understanding with basic robot operations. The challenges of multimodal alignment, richer constraint modeling, and robust dataset construction have been identified, highlighting opportunities for future integration with digital twins and automated assembly. Although the original system is still incomplete, the study concludes that a practical and impactful pipeline is achievable, demonstrating how artificial intelligence can help users recycle materials more effectively and contribute to sustainable, resource-saving designs.

AI search is changing how users seek information: instead of typing keywords and clicking through links, users increasingly ask complex questions and obtain direct answers on the results page. This shift, together with the rise of “zero-click search” and of chatbots based on Large Language Models (LLMs), is reshaping the customer experience of information seeking. This paper examines how LLM-based search systems are changing the way users retrieve information online, moving the dominant paradigm from keyword queries and ranked lists of links to direct answers in natural language. The study offers a structured, non-systematic narrative review comparing traditional search engines (represented by Google Search) and conversational AI tools (represented by ChatGPT and GPT-3/3.5-based search tools). It synthesises eight independent studies published between 2023 and 2026: three randomised controlled experiments, two large-scale observational analyses of real-world behaviour and three studies measuring content reliability, complemented by an industry benchmark (Vectara Hallucination Leaderboard). The analysis focuses on five key performance indicators (KPIs): number of queries per task (KPI 1), task success rate/accuracy (KPI 2), total time to task completion (KPI 3), rate of consultation of external sources/outbound clicks as a proxy for cross-verification (KPI 4), and the hallucination rate of AI systems compared with the rate of unreliable results in traditional search (KPI 5). AI systems consistently reduce task completion time, whereas the reduction in the number of queries depends on the task. Accuracy improves only when the generated output is correct; when it is wrong, accuracy drops sharply, consistent with a markedly lower consultation of external sources. The risk of error exists in both paradigms under specific conditions of use. The five KPIs should therefore be read as an interdependent system, with implications for the design of hybrid search tools in human-computer interaction and information retrieval.

Accurate biomechanical modeling is essential for assessing musculoskeletal loading during occupational tasks, but traditional laboratory motion capture is often impractical for field applications. This study developed and evaluated a sensor fusion framework combining flexible wearable sensors with single-view mobile video keypoints for biomechanical modeling of simulated wind turbine maintenance operations. Eighteen healthy participants performed three tasks: symmetric lifting, bolt-torque tensioning, and ladder climbing. Motion was captured simultaneously using 13 BioStamp flexible sensors, a marker-based motion capture system, and mobile video processed with pose detection algorithms. A convolutional neural network was trained using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation to predict whole-body joint angles referenced to OpenSim inverse kinematics. The fusion model achieved an average RMSE of 9.3°, improving estimation accuracy by 5% compared with the sensor-only model and 21% compared with the video-only model. Findings suggest that combining flexible sensors with video-derived keypoints offers a scalable approach for field-based occupational biomechanics assessment.

Collaborative robots, designed to work alongside humans in shared environments, are transforming manufacturing production lines, enabling partial automation and boosting productivity. But their potential extends beyond these benefits. By implementing anticipatory strategies to prevent workers’ risky behaviours and reduce excessive workloads, collaborative robots can proactively enhance working conditions. For example, they can take on repetitive or strenuous tasks to reduce physical effort or adjust the pace of operations to help alleviate stress levels. Indeed, Musculoskeletal Disorders (MSDs) and Common Mental Disorders (CMDs), which arise from uncontrolled physical and cognitive loads, are major work-related health problems in developed countries, with incommensurate social and economic costs. Collaborative robots can curb the effect of such disorders and help in preserving workers’ health. This Chapter addresses how Human Factors and Ergonomics (HFE) can be monitored to provide robots with relevant inputs about the human state, and how robots can be employed to improve HFE. Novel strategies are proposed to adapt online robot behaviour to the workers’ psycho-physical state and enhance their well-being and productivity.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) hallucinations raise questions about how users respond to unreliable outputs from a technology on which they depend. Drawing on the cognitive–affective components of the Interaction of Person–Affect–Cognition–Execution (I-PACE) framework, this study examines the roles of GAI trust, cognitive dissonance, perceived controllability, and frustration in the relationship between perceived hallucinations and GAI dependence, with GAI literacy and self-efficacy as individual-difference moderators. A between-subjects experiment involved 546 participants who viewed the same GAI dialogue labelled as either containing fabricated information or verified as accurate. Participants in the former condition reported lower trust and perceived controllability, greater cognitive dissonance and frustration, and lower dependence scores. In the parallel model, the indirect associations through trust, controllability, and frustration were negative, whereas the indirect association through cognitive dissonance was positive. Higher GAI literacy weakened the positive controllability–dependence association. The remaining moderation hypotheses were not supported under the directional and multiplicity-adjusted criteria. The findings connect users’ evaluations of unreliable GAI responses with the difficulties they report in regulating their use. They underscore the importance of examining dependence alongside reliability judgements, cognitive conflict, and emotional reactions when assessing the human consequences of GAI hallucinations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract The increasing complexity of gallium nitride (GaN) semiconductor manufacturing has exposed the limitations of conventional factory automation, where isolated control systems, centralized decision-making, and human-dependent operations restrict production flexibility, scalability, and long-term optimization. This study proposes a next-generation AI-native architecture for a fully autonomous lights-out GaN semiconductor manufacturing facility that minimizes routine human involvement while enabling continuous, intelligent, and self-optimizing production. In the proposed framework, human participation is intentionally limited to exceptional engineering interventions, major equipment upgrades, regulatory compliance, and strategic decision-making, whereas all routine manufacturing activities are executed autonomously. The proposed architecture integrates distributed Edge AI, autonomous robotic systems, a deterministic industrial communication infrastructure, a real-time Digital Twin, and an AI Factory Operating System (AI-FOS) into a unified operational ecosystem. Unlike conventional smart factories that primarily automate predefined workflows, the proposed system enables perception, reasoning, adaptive decision-making, and continuous process optimization throughout the entire semiconductor production lifecycle, including wafer logistics, epitaxial growth, lithography, etching, metrology, testing, packaging, predictive maintenance, and energy orchestration. A key contribution of this work is the introduction of a distributed twelve-layer cognitive memory architecture, which provides every autonomous robot and intelligent manufacturing node with a common hierarchical decision framework. The architecture prioritizes life safety, environmental protection, anomaly recognition, experiential learning, quality optimization, equipment health monitoring, operational context awareness, asset management, maintenance planning, mission support, environmental signature analysis, and low-priority contextual knowledge. This shared cognitive framework enables consistent decision-making across heterogeneous robotic platforms while supporting continuous learning and knowledge reuse throughout the factory. The proposed architecture represents a shift from automation-centric manufacturing toward cognitive semiconductor production, where the factory operates as an intelligent, self-learning ecosystem rather than a collection of independently automated machines. By combining distributed artificial intelligence, cognitive robotics, Digital Twin technology, and deterministic industrial networking within a unified operating architecture, this work establishes a conceptual foundation for future autonomous semiconductor fabrication facilities designed to achieve high production efficiency, enhanced safety, continuous adaptability, and scalable operation with minimal human intervention. https://dynisos.com/
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) can add demographic identities when workplace descriptions leave identity unspecified. We audited nine live model configurations using 20 experimental and five control phrases, with 50 stateless generations per model–phrase cell at temperature 1.0 (11,250 responses). The experimental conditions bundled role content with communicative register: authority/resource-control phrases were direct or directive, whereas coordination/assistance phrases were reporting, deferential, or permission-seeking. The design therefore estimates a role-and-register contrast, not a causal effect of occupational status alone. Both conditions were majority female: full-grid attribution was 63.58% female, 35.89% male, 0.47% nonbinary, and 0.07% unparsed in the authority/directive condition, versus 92.62%, 6.04%, 1.20%, and 0.13%, respectively, in the support/deferential condition. Model risk differences ranged from − 12.2 to + 93.6 percentage points. A Paule–Mandel random-effects synthesis showed extreme heterogeneity (I2 = 98.6% on the log-odds scale; 95% prediction interval for the odds ratio, 0.014–63,659), so no stable common model effect is claimed. A cross-classified block bootstrap retaining 50-response cells estimated an aggregate male-attribution gap of 29.9 points (95% CI, 6.0–55.6). Name entropy diagnostics documented substantial within-cell repetition. Control mismatches were predominantly explicit model outputs rather than parser failures; excluding models below 80% control agreement did not reverse the aggregate gap. Name-based race inference is confined to a reliability appendix. The results identify heterogeneous demographic defaults under this prompt bundle and motivate crossed role-by-register experiments.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract The targeted discovery of inorganic materials remains challenging due to the vastness of compositional design spaces and the high cost of exhaustive screening. Task-specific generative artificial intelligence represents a particularly efficient alternative to screening, yet demands tedious collection of training data before providing real benefit. General-purpose large language models (LLMs) have recently shown tremendous potential for the targeted generation of single, optimal materials compositions without the need for task-specific fine-tuning. However, it is unclear whether LLMs generally pose an advantage compared to specialized generative models, in particular in large design spaces. Here, we demonstrate that such models are capable of covering entire regions of the targeted property space effectively and systematically. Using Elpasolite materials as an established benchmark for generative tasks in large chemical spaces, we find that an iterative prompt-and-response framework is able to recover on average 96% of all low-energy Elpasolites in the target region. This performance, driven mainly by iterative in-context learning, surpasses the generative abilities of previous, task-specific models. Our results establish general-purpose LLMs as flexible and accessible components for inverse materials design workflows.

Reinforcement learning has become the foundational paradigm for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Yet the dominant approach, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), relies on a geometrically degenerate clipping proxy that cannot adapt its resistance to policy shifts, leading to premature clipping and degraded exploration. Subsequent variants alleviate these issues through fragmented and heuristic modifications. We propose Generalized Proximal Policy Optimization (GPPO), a principled and unified framework for understanding and designing LLM RL algorithms through the lens of divergence. We establish a generalized $f$-divergence trust-region theory with a monotonic performance improvement guarantee, and show that different $f$-divergences induce distinct geometries and policy update dynamics. We further introduce novel estimator topologies that provide more faithful divergence estimates than the conventional single-sample Monte Carlo estimation. Under this framework, PPO and recent variants such as DAPO, DPPO, and RIPO emerge as special cases, establishing a principled two-dimensional design space of {Divergence $\times$ Estimator}. Extensive experiments on eight competition-level math and coding benchmarks show that both dimensions are critical. The best-performing GPPO instantiation surpasses standard GRPO by up to 50% and 14% on math and coding, delivering SOTA performance.

This article theoretically examines the pedagogical and methodological opportunities, organizational mechanisms, and didactic conditions for developing students’ independent learning activities in vocational education institutions through the use of generative artificial intelligence technologies. The research findings present methodological recommendations developed on the basis of theoretical analysis and substantiate the need for further experimental studies to determine their empirical effectiveness.

The public release of ChatGPT presents language education with both advantages and challenges. Being widely available and readily producing texts at user's command, it is an especially useful resource in ESL writing. However, to be able to leverage it effectively for that purpose, we need to understand the writing micro-processes surrounding its use. To this end, this study investigates, through an experimental design, writing micro-processes along with writing outcomes, and perceptions of 12 ESL writers across three writing conditions. The data included interviews, questionnaires as well as essay grades and screen recordings. Two of the three conditions involved the use of ChatGPT. The results indicate that the majority of participants favored the ChatGPT- assisted conditions and noted its role in aiding idea generation. Despite this preference, some participants noted that ChatGPT-produced texts felt robotic and lacked a human touch. We found no statistically significant differences across the three conditions in the participants' essays. Most notably, our analysis identified distinct clusters of writing micro-processes associated with the ChatGPT conditions, suggesting that generative AI tools can influence writing behaviors although the link to outcomes is not straightforward. These findings provide insights into the potential benefits and limitations of using AI tools in writing tasks. The article discusses areas for further research to enhance the integration of AI into ESL writing education.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is redefining marketing communication by extending the discipline beyond human-driven creativity into a data-supported, emotionally responsive, and context-aware domain. Unlike traditional AI focused on automation and analytics, generative AI enables personalized content creation, immersive brand storytelling, and adaptive consumer engagement. This chapter examines generative AI as a creative paradigm through the lenses of neuromarketing, cognitive psychology, and consumer behavior, highlighting how large language models, visual generators, and multimodal systems support “machine creativity.” It further discusses measurement approaches like EEG, eye-tracking, and AI-based sentiment analysis that may be used to assess emotional impact. Ethical concerns such as privacy, consent, and transparency are discussed in light of emerging governance frameworks. The chapter concludes by considering future integration in VR, AR, and metaverse environments and emphasizes a collaborative balance between human creativity and AI-driven innovation.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is transforming entrepreneurship by helping entrepreneurs generate ideas, analyze information, create content, develop business models, support marketing, and make decisions. This review examines the growing role of GenAI in entrepreneurial activities, with a focus on opportunity recognition, creativity, innovation, SMEs, emerging economies, and responsible AI use. GenAI can reduce resource constraints and provide affordable support to small businesses, but challenges such as inaccurate information, overdependence, privacy concerns, and unequal digital skills remain. The article highlights the importance of human–AI collaboration and introduces the concept of AI entrepreneurial capability, which includes AI literacy, effective prompting, evaluation of AI outputs, decision-making, and responsible use of AI. The review concludes that future entrepreneurship should focus not only on using AI to generate more opportunities but also on improving the quality, sustainability, and responsible development of those opportunities.

documents.abstract: BackgroundWork-related musculoskeletal disorders are a major occupational health concern, and REBA is widely used to evaluate postural risk. The role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in REBA scoring remains insufficiently examined.ObjectiveTo explore REBA scoring differences between a certified human ergonomist and three generative AI systems under controlled multimodal input conditions.MethodsSeventy-seven anonymized posture images from four task categories were evaluated by a human reference evaluator and ChatGPT, Gemini, and Wrtn. Identical images and standardized posture descriptors were provided to the AI systems. REBA scores were compared using repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni-adjusted post-hoc comparisons.ResultsSignificant rater, body-part, and rater × body-part effects were observed. Wrtn generated comparatively higher trunk and wrist scores and lower scores for the lower arm, Gemini generated comparatively higher Final REBA scores, and ChatGPT produced comparatively lower scores across several body regions.ConclusionsGenerative AI systems showed systematic body-region-specific differences in REBA scoring relative to the human reference evaluator. These exploratory findings indicate the need for further validation and expert oversight before AI-assisted REBA assessment is used in workplace practice.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: This chapter examines the implications of generative artificial intelligence for assessment practices, academic integrity and quality assurance in South African higher education institutions. As AI-powered tools such as ChatGPT, SciSpace, Gemini, and Copilot become embedded in teaching, learning and assessment, they offer opportunities to enhance efficiency, feedback and assessment design while raising ethical concerns about misconduct, authorship, transparency and assessment validity. Drawing on the Theory of Planned Behaviour and the Utilitarian Theory of Ethics, the chapter adopts a conceptual and critical approach to analyse how the literature portrays academics' and students' perceptions, adoption and justification of the ethical or unethical use of generative artificial intelligence in assessment contexts. Particular attention is given to challenges surrounding originality, intellectual property, and authenticity, which, in turn, have implications for assessment outcomes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND: Breast symmetry and harmony remain challenging goals in aesthetic breast surgery. Preoperative marking is fundamental for planning; however, most techniques rely on nipple-areola complex (NAC) distances and subjective visual assessment, often neglecting thoracic width, height, and the true breast footprint. A geometric framework based on harmonic proportions can help standardize preoperative planning and may improve the reproducibility of breast markings. METHODS: A two-dimensional geometric template was developed by integrating constant anatomical references (sternum, clavicles, axillary and acromial lines, and umbilicus) with proportional relationships derived from aesthetic and anthropometric studies. The template was calibrated for each patient's using thoracic width and height and was designed to be superimposed on standardized frontal photographs. It guides the NAC position, breast width, upper pole contour, and inframammary fold level. The model was applied in mastopexy and reduction mammaplasty as a preoperative planning and postoperative photographic overlay comparison, as well as a visual aid in resident teaching sessions. RESULTS: The template was easily incorporated into daily practice using standard clinical photographs and simple digital overlays. Geometric gridlines and proportional curves allowed visualization of the NAC position, breast symmetry, and contour in relation to thoracic dimensions. Repeated overlays facilitated the longitudinal comparison of breast position and shape. During teaching sessions, the template was used as a visual aid to facilitate resident understanding of the geometric relationships between thoracic anatomy, the breast footprint, and marking decisions. CONCLUSIONS: This innovative geometric template offers a simple, visually intuitive tool for standardizing preoperative marking and supporting postoperative photographic overlay comparisons in breast surgeries. It is inexpensive, compatible with existing photographic workflows, and may support training and future digital or artificial intelligence integration. Prospective studies are needed to quantify the impact of these factors on aesthetic outcomes and learning curves.
